title: Shein Slashes IPO Valuation to $25 Billion as Growth Stalls Ahead of Hong Kong Debut
excerpt: The fast-fashion giant's planned listing values it at a quarter of its 2022 peak as tariffs, EU fees, and slowing sales erode investor confidence.
body:
• Shein is targeting a company valuation of approximately $25 billion in its Hong Kong IPO, down from $98.2 billion in a 2022 fundraising round
  • Revenue growth decelerated sharply from 41.1% in 2023 to just 1.1% in Q1 2026, as the end of U.S. de minimis exemptions and new EU import fees hit its business model
  • The company swung to a $99 million quarterly loss in Q1 2026, compared with net income of $395 million a year earlier
  • Shein plans to issue up to 8% of its total shares, which would translate to an offering size of up to $2 billion

Shein, the Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer known for $5 dresses and $10 jeans, is set to launch its long-delayed initial public offering in Hong Kong at a valuation roughly a quarter of what investors assigned it just four years ago.

The company is now targeting a valuation of around $25 billion, according to Reuters, citing sources familiar with the deal. That figure has slid from $30 billion to $40 billion just weeks earlier, and marks a dramatic retreat from the $98.2 billion valuation Shein commanded in a 2022 fundraising round when it was first pursuing a New York listing.

Tariffs and Trade Barriers Take Their Toll

The steep markdown reflects a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape for cross-border e-commerce platforms that relied on shipping cheap goods directly from China to consumers worldwide.

The United States ended its de minimis exemption for small parcels last year, removing a key advantage of Shein's direct-shipping model and forcing the company to invest in local warehousing. In July, the European Union imposed a €3 fee on low-value e-commerce imports, further raising costs in a market that accounts for roughly a third of Shein's revenue.

"The problem is that the company is already on a downward trajectory. E-commerce competition is extremely intense, both in China and overseas."

— Eddie Tam, CIO, Central Asset Investments

Revenue growth decelerated from 41.1% in 2023 to 20.7% in 2024, then to 8% in 2025 for total revenue of $41.8 billion. In the first quarter of 2026, growth slowed further to just 1.1%. Net income fell 39% to $2.06 billion in 2025 before the company swung to a $99 million loss in Q1 2026, partly due to a $328 million fair-value charge on convertible preferred shares.

Investor Skepticism Runs Deep

Some investors who attended IPO presentations told Reuters they were not convinced Shein could return to the growth rates that once justified its near-$100 billion valuation. Research firm Coresight expects growth to slow to around 2% this year as trade policy headwinds persist.

At a $25 billion valuation, Shein would trade at roughly 12 times its 2025 earnings and approximately 0.6 times sales — below Swedish rival H&M at about 1.1 times sales and far below Zara parent Inditex at 4.6 times. The discount reflects concerns about lower margins and weaker earnings visibility.

The lower valuation also creates complications for existing investors. Under the terms of Shein's IPO filing, the company would be required to provide extra shares to certain pre-IPO investors if the valuation falls below agreed thresholds.

Customer Growth Without Depth

While Shein's annual active customers rose to 273 million in 2025 from 230 million a year earlier, purchase frequency remained flat at roughly four orders per year. The figures suggest the company continues to attract shoppers but has not deepened engagement.

Shein ramped marketing spending to $1.43 billion in Q1 2026 from $1.09 billion a year earlier, and will need to demonstrate that the investment is translating into sustainable demand growth rather than simply buying eyeballs.

The company won approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission for its Hong Kong listing on July 10, after failed listing attempts in both New York and London. Shein plans to use IPO proceeds for technology investments, global brand-building, and general corporate purposes.
